findings.headline: Re-acquisition budget for equity share and shared ownership properties increased for a higher than anticipated number of properties re-acquired in 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper describes this budget as demand-led, depending on how many properties are offered back to the council and on market values. Re-acquired properties are then marketed for resale.
findings.matters: Demand-led re-acquisition budgets that rise with the number of properties offered back show a cost driver that other councils with shared ownership stock will recognise.
findings.figures: Revised 'Other' HRA budget £650k in 2026/27 and £150k a year thereafter
findings.quote: The increase in budget provision reflects a higher than anticipated number of properties being re-acquired during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Round 4 Local Authority Housing Fund grant secured, covering approximately 45% of acquisition costs for six homes
findings.detail: Two properties are to be acquired in 2026/27 and four in 2028/29. Four homes will be used for temporary accommodation and two to support refugee resettlement. The remaining costs come from the unallocated New Build provision.
findings.matters: External grant covering a set share of acquisition costs is a funding mix other councils using LAHF rounds will compare.
findings.figures: approximately 45% of acquisition costs; six homes
findings.quote: The LAHF grant will fund approximately 45% of the acquisition costs

findings.headline: £5.32 million MHCLG water efficiency grant held in capital reserves, with £56,000 spent in 2025/26 and £2.684 million forecast in 2026/27
findings.detail: The grant funds water-saving initiatives across the Cambridge area through to 2032. The paper gives a spending profile of £2.578 million forecast for 2027/28 after the 2026/27 spend.
findings.matters: Grant money ring-fenced within reserves and drawn down on a published profile is a reserve position other councils with similar grants would compare.
findings.figures: £5.32 million grant; £56,000 spent 2025/26; £2.684 million forecast 2026/27; £2.578 million forecast 2027/28
findings.quote: the £5.32 million grant funding currently secured and held within the council’s capital reserves

findings.headline: Northstowe Civic Hub forecast at £29.814 million total, with £16.5 million expected from Section 106 contributions
findings.detail: Planning and design commenced in 2025/26, with capital investment continuing over the following four years of the programme. The paper describes the hub as a significant strategic investment in civic and community infrastructure.
findings.matters: Large community infrastructure dependent on developer contributions shows how a council's capital programme relies on S106 timing and receipts.
findings.figures: £29.814 million total forecast; £16.5 million from Section 106 contributions
findings.quote: Total expenditure is forecast to amount to £29.814 million, of which £16.5 million is expected to be funded through Section 106 contributions.

findings.headline: £9.2 million to be advanced to SCIP during 2026/27 for the Cambium Square joint venture delivering 256 low-carbon homes
findings.detail: The paper says the development is jointly funded by the council and the Hill Group, with financial returns expected on completion and sale. The advance is in line with the approved business plan and project cashflow.
findings.matters: Cash advanced into a joint venture with returns deferred to sale is an exposure that finance directors and lenders assess separately from direct capital spend.
findings.figures: £9.2 million advanced to SCIP in 2026/27; 256 homes
findings.quote: It is currently forecast that £9.2 million will be advanced to SCIP during 2026/27

findings.headline: Ermine Street Housing investment fund of £2.272 million brings the council's total investment in the company to the £120 million ceiling
findings.detail: The paper says the funding gives the company flexibility to respond to investment opportunities and to acquire homes, including for single people. It describes the investment as supporting the council's housing objectives.
findings.matters: A company investment reaching its approved ceiling is a point where any further support needs a new decision, which other councils with arm's-length housing companies would note.
findings.figures: £2.272 million investment fund; £120 million ceiling
findings.quote: will bring the council’s total investment in the company up to the £120 million ceiling previously approved by Council

findings.headline: Revised HRA borrowing of £52,966k in 2026/27 and £39,694k in 2027/28, falling to nil by 2030/31
findings.detail: The paper says investment levels in the HRA New Build Programme beyond the first years depend on the refreshed 30-year Business Plan, which will assess the HRA's ability to accommodate further borrowing. Later-year expenditure has been phased to fit within the existing financial framework.
findings.matters: A borrowing path that depends on a pending business plan review is a sensitivity other HRA finance teams and lenders would track.
findings.quote: dependent on the outcome of the refreshed 30-year Business Plan

findings.headline: General Fund borrowing costs estimated at £0.506 million of revenue cost for 2027/28, based on an interest rate of 5.06%
findings.detail: The estimate covers the General Fund capital programme including existing approvals. The paper gives General Fund borrowing of £10,000k in each year from 2026/27 to 2030/31 in its revised financing table.
findings.matters: The revenue cost of borrowing at a stated rate is the number a finance director needs to test the affordability of a borrowing-funded programme.
findings.figures: £0.506 million revenue cost 2027/28; 5.06% interest rate; General Fund borrowing £10,000k a year
findings.quote: The total estimated cost to revenue for the borrowing costs of the GF capital programme (including existing approvals) is £0.506 million for 2027/2028.

findings.headline: Retained Right to Buy receipts for reinvestment forecast at £0.75 million in 2026/27, against £5.7 million in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper says capital receipts now come mainly from new-build shared ownership sales, with Right to Buy sales no longer a significant funding source. It states that this increases the programme's reliance on PWLB borrowing and places greater emphasis on alternative funding.
findings.matters: A sharp fall in receipts that funded housing investment is a shift that other councils with Right to Buy income are also tracking, and it moves cost onto borrowing.
findings.figures: £0.75 million forecast 2026/27; £5.7 million in 2025/26
findings.quote: The 2026/27 forecast assumes £0.75 million of retained Right to Buy receipts available for reinvestment in new housing

findings.headline: Three further HRA developments added to the programme, expected to deliver 125 affordable homes, funded from unallocated provision
findings.detail: The schemes are Northstowe Phase 2C (82 rented homes), Cottenham Rampton Road Phase B (12 rented and 2 shared-ownership homes) and Northstowe Phase 2D (29 rented homes). The paper says they will be funded from provision already within the approved programme.
findings.matters: Adding schemes from existing unallocated provision rather than new borrowing shows how an HRA programme can expand within an approved envelope.
findings.figures: 125 affordable homes (82 + 12 rented and 2 shared-ownership + 29 rented)
findings.quote: are expected to deliver a further 125 affordable homes

findings.headline: £11.3 million of HRA New Build budget rephased into 2026/27 after slower developer progress in 2025/26, with spend since brought forward from later years
findings.detail: The paper attributes the 2025/26 rephasing to slower than anticipated developer progress. It states that progress has since accelerated across a number of sites, allowing expenditure to be brought forward from later years.
findings.matters: Reliance on developer delivery timing shows how a single year's slippage can move a large housing budget between years.
findings.figures: £11.3 million rephased into 2026/27; HRA New Build revised budget £55,182k in 2026/27 and £38,321k in 2027/28
findings.quote: Slower than anticipated progress by developers during the 2025/26 programme resulted in £11.3 million of budget provision being rephased into 2026/27.

findings.headline: £4.0 million of refuse collection vehicle replacement expenditure reprofiled from 2026/27 into 2027/28
findings.detail: The paper says the electric fleet replacement has been aligned with the commissioning and operational readiness of the WREN facility. It describes the change as giving lead-in time for procurement and infrastructure integration, and as mitigating risks to service continuity.
findings.matters: A fleet electrification timetable that slips to match energy infrastructure is a timing pressure other councils running similar transitions will recognise.
findings.figures: £4.0 million reprofiled from 2026/27 to 2027/28
findings.quote: £4.0 million of expenditure originally forecast for 2026/27 is now proposed to be reprofiled into 2027/28

findings.headline: WREN renewable energy facility is connected to the electricity grid, with formal launch expected in December 2026 or January 2027
findings.detail: The paper says testing and commissioning are underway, including checks on electricity flows and battery storage performance. Launch is subject to successful completion of these activities. £5.786 million has been approved for the project from 2025/26, with £4.167 million forecast across 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, can see a grid-connected energy scheme moving towards launch against a defined approved budget and forecast spend.
findings.figures: £5.786 million approved; £4.167 million forecast across 2026/27 and 2027/28; launch December 2026 or January 2027
findings.quote: the WREN facility is now connected to the electricity grid

findings.headline: Council Tax is forecast to rise from £12,865k in 2026-27 to £15,618k in 2031-32, the only funding line in the table that grows in every year.
findings.detail: The table shows council tax increasing each year across the five-year forecast. It is the sole funding line that increases steadily, while government grants reduce or end over the same period.
findings.matters: A council that is increasingly reliant on council tax as grants fall is a useful comparison point for finance directors and lenders assessing the mix of funding across the sector.
findings.quote: Council Tax (12,865)

findings.headline: The 2026-27 Adjustment Support Grant of £2,336k and the Collection Fund surplus of £1,302k are not forecast to recur from 2027-28.
findings.detail: Both lines appear only in 2026-27 and are shown as nil in every later year of the table. They are one-off items within the current year's funding.
findings.matters: Non-recurring funding that supports the current year and drops out of the forecast is a common source of later budget gaps, and peers and lenders will look at how much of the base budget depends on one-off items.
findings.figures: Adjustment Support Grant: £2,336k in 2026-27, nil thereafter; Collection Fund (Surplus) / Deficit: £1,302k in 2026-27, nil thereafter
findings.quote: Adjustment Support Grant (2,336)

findings.headline: Transitional Protection (Damping Payment) is forecast at £2,290k in 2027-28, £4,338k in 2028-29 and £1,329k in 2029-30, then nil from 2030-31.
findings.detail: The table shows a time-limited damping payment that peaks in 2028-29 and ends after 2029-30. The forecast assumes no damping support from 2030-31.
findings.matters: Damping payments that end on a fixed schedule create a known cliff in funding, which a finance director would need to plan around and a lender would want to see reflected in the forecast.
findings.quote: Transitional Protection (Damping Payment)

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant is forecast to fall from £10,547k in 2026-27 to £7,800k in 2027-28 and £4,966k in 2028-29, before rising to £6,112k.
findings.detail: The table shows the grant reducing sharply over the first two years of the forecast. It then recovers partially in 2029-30 and holds at the same level in 2031-32.
findings.matters: Revenue Support Grant is a central funding line, and a fall of this size over two years is the kind of change that the Fair Funding Review context in the paper relates to and that peers will face on similar terms.
findings.quote: Revenue Support Grant (10,547)

findings.headline: The paper says contributions to earmarked reserves, which it describes as 'significant' historically, are 'unlikely' to be possible because of the Fair Funding Review.
findings.detail: The footnote notes that net operating expenditure includes appropriations to earmarked reserves. It states that these appropriations have historically been significant and that it is unlikely this will be possible due to the Fair Funding Review.
findings.matters: A council that has relied on reserve appropriations to balance its budget and now expects to stop doing so is a signal for lenders and peers that the reserve buffer may stop being rebuilt.
findings.quote: Operating Expenditure also includes appropriations to earmarked reserves which historically have been significant.

findings.headline: The MTFS net position moves from (£2,522k) in 2026-27 to £526k in 2028-29 and £5,205k in 2031-32.
findings.detail: The table shows net operating expenditure set against government grants and council tax, with a 'Total Net Position' line. The footnote states that further service pressures would 'exaggerate the funding gap' and should be managed within existing budgets where possible.
findings.matters: A finance director at this council or a peer can see the forecast turning from a surplus in 2026-27 to a growing shortfall from 2028-29 onward, and the council itself flags that pressures could widen it.
findings.quote: *Further service pressures will, however, exaggerate the funding gap

findings.matters: A council tax premium policy delivering its full forecast is a concrete, reproducible income source that finance directors at other councils may be considering.

findings.matters: Vacancy in a commercial property portfolio shows up as an in-year income shortfall, and a finance director elsewhere will want to know how far the timing slips.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Rent Setting and Service Charge Policy 1
findings.headline: Affordable Rents in South Cambridgeshire villages are capped at 70% of gross median market rent, and at 60% on Cambridge City fringe sites
findings.detail: The policy sets the affordable rent ceiling in villages at the lower of 70% of gross median market rent or the Local Housing Allowance rate, and at the lower of 60% of Cambridge City market rent or the LHA rate on City fringe sites. Government policy allows up to 80% of market rent, and the policy describes the lower percentages as maintaining affordability.
findings.matters: Setting affordable rents below the 80% government maximum determines the rental income that new affordable-rent stock can generate, which affects the viability assumptions for development funded on that basis.
findings.figures: 70% (villages); 60% (City fringe); up to 80% (government maximum)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Rent Setting and Service Charge Policy 1
findings.headline: South Cambridgeshire does not apply the high-income tenant rent provisions that would allow rents up to market level
findings.detail: The policy says the Council does not operate a high-income tenant rent policy and does not charge higher rents based on household income. It gives the reason as avoiding a disincentive for tenants to increase their earnings. The policy notes that Government provisions could allow higher rents, potentially up to market rent, for tenants above a prescribed income threshold.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender reviewing HRA income, would want to know that this available income lever is not being used.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: The Council does not currently operate a high-income tenant rent policy and does not charge higher rents based on a tenant’s household income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Rent Setting and Service Charge Policy 1
findings.headline: The current Government rent settlement permits annual rent increases of up to CPI plus 1% for ten years from 1 April 2026
findings.detail: The policy states that annual rent changes are proposed within the national rent policy and the Rent Standard, subject to Council approval through the annual budget process. It records the current settlement as CPI plus 1% for a ten-year period, and says the Council will apply whatever requirements are in force at the time if policy changes.
findings.matters: This sets the ceiling on annual HRA rent income growth that the Council can plan against over a decade, which is a core assumption for lenders and for housing finance planning elsewhere.
findings.figures: CPI plus 1%; ten-year period commencing 1 April 2026
findings.quote: The current Government rent settlement permits annual increases of up to Consumer Price Index (CPI) plus 1% for a ten-year period commencing on 1 April 2026.

findings.headline: The Northstowe Civic Hub is revised to £3,736k for 2026-27 from a £4,000k budget, and S106 funding for Northstowe is revised to £1,725k from £5,000k
findings.detail: The Civic Hub is one of the Northstowe housing-related capital lines. Its funding comes partly from a section 106 contribution ring-fenced for housing, which the paper describes as used for Northstowe. Both the spend and the S106 figure are lower in the revised 2026-27 column than in the budget.
findings.matters: A council whose Northstowe spend depends on developer contributions carries the risk that the contributions arrive later or in smaller amounts, and this paper shows a lower S106 figure for 2026-27 than budgeted.
findings.figures: Civic Hub £4,000k budget 2026-27 and £3,736k revised 2026-27; £9,192k in 2027-28; S106 contribution £5,000k budget 2026-27 and £1,725k revised 2026-27; £5,212k 2027-28
findings.quote: S106 Agreement Contribution (ring fenced for Housing) - used for Northstowe (5,000) (1,725) (5,212) (5,132) (600)

findings.headline: Vehicle Sinking Fund is shown as a financing source of £2,784k in the 2026-27 budget and £1,529k in the revised column
findings.detail: The Vehicle Sinking Fund is one of several earmarked reserves used to finance the capital programme, drawn in each year to 2031-32. The paper lists it among the financing lines, not as a separate reserves statement, so the balance remaining is not shown.
findings.matters: Using earmarked reserves to fund vehicle replacement spreads the cost over time, and a finance director at another council can compare how much of its own sinking fund is committed to the same kind of spend.

findings.headline: Capital receipts used to finance the programme are revised to £4,688k for 2026-27 from a £3,033k budget
findings.detail: Capital receipts are shown as a funding source in every year of the programme. The 2026-27 figure is higher in the revised column than in the budget column, and the table shows £7,343k for 2027-28.
findings.matters: A council relying on asset sales to fund capital spending is exposed if receipts arrive later or lower than planned, and the revised figure shows the reliance has increased for 2026-27.

findings.headline: External borrowing is revised to £11,463k for 2026-27 from a £10,000k budget, with £10,000k a year shown for 2027-28 to 2030-31
findings.detail: The Investment line of £10,000k a year is funded by external borrowing. The revised 2026-27 borrowing is £1,463k above the budget figure. No borrowing is shown in 2031-32.
findings.matters: Each year's external borrowing is a new funding requirement that the council must find, and the revised 2026-27 figure is above its original budget.
findings.figures: £10,000k budget 2026-27; £11,463k revised 2026-27; £10,000k for each of 2027-28 to 2030-31; Investment £10,000k budget 2026-27 and £11,463k revised

findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure for 2026-27 is revised to £31,068k from a budget of £38,202k
findings.detail: The total General Fund capital programme is shown with a 2026-27 budget and a revised 2026-27 figure, followed by budgets for 2027-28 to 2031-32. The table does not state the reasons for the revision.
findings.matters: A finance director, or a lender reading the council's borrowing need, can compare the revised programme against the original budget to see how much spending has moved between years.

findings.headline: CPI forecast to peak at around 5.0% during 2027, against 3.5% in September 2026, per the November 2026 MPC forecast
findings.detail: The report cites the November 2026 MPC forecast, which expects CPI to peak at about 5.0% during 2027 mainly from higher energy prices, before falling toward 2% over the medium term. Earlier in the report, CPI is put at 3.5% in September 2026 with a peak of around 3.6% in the final quarter of 2026, and the report treats inflation as a key risk to the forecasts.
findings.matters: A peak of about 5.0% in 2027 raises cost and pay pressure on every council's budget, and the difference between the two peak estimates is a gap that other councils' forecasts may need to reconcile.
findings.figures: CPI 3.5% in September 2026; peak around 3.6% in Q4 2026 (paragraph 10); peak around 5.0% during 2027 (MPC November 2026 forecast); MPC table 4.9% in Q2 2027
findings.quote: peaking at around 5.0% during 2027

findings.headline: Council Tax Support Scheme under review, with no assumed financial outcome in the MTFS
findings.detail: The council is reviewing its Council Tax Support Scheme to meet residents' needs, improve administrative efficiency and align with other authorities where appropriate. The report says no assumptions about the outcome are in the current forecasts, and that any financial implications will come to Cabinet and Council in February 2027.
findings.matters: Changes to local council tax support affect the council tax base and collection, which a finance director would want to see costed before February 2027.
findings.figures: no figure given; implications to be reported February 2027
findings.quote: No assumptions regarding the outcome of the review have been reflected in the current MTFS forecasts.

findings.headline: MTFS includes no assumptions for the proposed Development Company (DevCo) or Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The report says no assumptions have been included for the proposed Development Company, because its business model, delivery arrangements and financial implications are still being developed. It also says no reorganisation assumptions are included after the Government paused elements of LGR on 7 September, with Cambridgeshire & Peterborough decisions not expected until early 2027.
findings.matters: Costs, income or savings from DevCo or reorganisation would sit outside the reported gap, which matters to anyone reading the forecast as a full position.

findings.quote: No assumptions have been included within the MTFS in relation to the proposed Development Company (DevCo).

findings.headline: General Fund borrowing is predominantly undertaken on a short-term basis, typically for periods of up to two years
findings.detail: The report says General Fund borrowing is mostly short-term and that the MTFS assumes borrowing rates will remain above the forecast Bank Rate. The table of inflation assumptions gives a 5% borrowing interest assumption for 2027/28 and a 4.2% investment interest assumption.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing exposes the council to refinancing and rate movements in each cycle, which matters to a lender assessing its refinancing risk.

findings.detail: The report says the 2027/28 settlement includes £7.8 million of Revenue Support Grant and £2.3 million of Transitional Protection Funding. The transitional funding is intended to phase the Fair Funding Review 2.0 impact over three years. The report also says general grant funding has continued to decline over the years.
findings.matters: Transitional funding that runs for three years creates a future step-down that other councils adopting Fair Funding 2.0 will also face.

findings.quote: £7.8 million of Revenue Support Grant and £2.3 million of Transitional Protection Funding have been included in the 2027/28 settlement.

findings.detail: The funding table shows the HRA capital financing requirement and prudential borrowing line at £49,277k in the 2026-27 budget column and £52,966k in the revised column. findings.matters: A £3,689k increase in in-year borrowing for the HRA is a direct change in the council's debt requirement, which lenders and finance directors at peer councils would track when comparing borrowing against capital plans.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 241126 - Rent Setting & Service Charge Policy
findings.headline: The policy clarifies how Affordable Rents are set on newly acquired or developed homes within larger schemes
findings.detail: The paper says the clarification aims to price comparable properties in the same development, phase or parcel on a consistent basis, so that rent differences do not arise solely from the timing of first lettings relative to the annual rent increase. The paper states the policy otherwise largely reflects existing practice.
findings.matters: How Affordable Rents are set on new homes determines rental income from a council's development programme, which other councils with new-build programmes would also need to consider.
findings.quote: it clarifies the methodology for establishing Affordable Rents on newly acquired or developed homes within larger schemes.

findings.matters: The rent uplift ceiling sets the HRA's main income growth parameter for the decade, which a finance director at this or any council with a housing revenue account would need to model.

findings.detail: The liquidity table shows Ermine St Housing as the largest long-term investment, ahead of SCIP at 12% and the Council's local authority lending at 14%. Total investments were £177,055k at 30 September 2026.
findings.matters: A single related-entity loan making up two-thirds of the portfolio is a concentration that lenders and peer finance teams would look at when assessing the council's exposure to that entity.
findings.figures: £117,728k Ermine St Housing; 66% of portfolio; total investments £177,055k; SCIP £20,859k (12%)
findings.quote: Ermine St Housing

findings.headline: Bail-in exposure rose from nil to £5,100k at 30 September 2026, primarily from a fixed term deposit with a UK clearing bank.
findings.detail: The paper says this diversifies the portfolio but adds exposure to bail-in risk. It notes exposure may increase in future quarters if more funds go to banks and building societies.
findings.matters: Bail-in exposure determines how a council's cash would rank in a bank failure, which lenders and other councils weigh when setting counterparty policy.
findings.figures: £5,100k bail-in exposure at 30 September 2026, up from nil at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: primarily due to a fixed term deposit with a UK clearing bank.

findings.headline: Commercial property rental income (net) is forecast at £2,069k against a £2,294k budget, £225k below, due to vacant suites in one investment property.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the shortfall to vacant suites within one of the Council's investment properties.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is a revenue stream many councils depend on, and vacancy-driven shortfalls are a known pressure on that income.
findings.figures: £2,294k budget; £2,069k forecast outturn; £225k variance
findings.quote: Separately, commercial property income is expected to be below budget due to vacant suites within one of the Council's investment properties.

findings.headline: Investment income is forecast at £6,844k against a £6,476k budget, £368k above budget.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the higher forecast to sustained higher rates from money market funds and lending to other local authorities. It says the original estimate assumed at least one 25 basis point Base Rate cut in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council earning more on cash than budgeted, while its interest payable rises, shows how the net position is moving against the original assumptions.
findings.figures: £6,476k budget; £6,844k forecast outturn; £368k variance; 25 basis point cut assumed in original estimate
findings.quote: Investment income is forecast to exceed the original budget, driven by sustained higher interest rates offered by money market funds and lending to other Local Authorities.

findings.headline: Bank Rate has stayed at 3.75% through the first half of 2026/27, against a 2026/27 budget that assumed further cuts.
findings.detail: The paper says markets are now pricing in up to four Base Rate increases over the next 12 months if hostilities continue. Treasury advisers MUFG and Capital Economics expect rates to peak at 4.0% or 4.25%.
findings.matters: A budget built on rate cuts that is now facing rate rises affects both investment income and borrowing costs at the same time, which is a position other councils may be in.
findings.figures: 3.75% Bank Rate; peak expectations of 4.0% or 4.25%; up to four base rate increases priced over 12 months
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget had assumed further cuts in interest rates.

findings.headline: Interest payable is forecast at £3,447k against a £3,131k budget, a £316k variance, which the paper attributes to changed market expectations for Bank Rate.
findings.detail: The paper links the higher forecast to market expectations of Bank Rate movements, driven by inflation and geopolitical uncertainty. It describes the rise in expectations as stemming from ongoing inflationary pressures and geopolitical uncertainty.
findings.matters: Interest cost forecasts that move against budget mid-year show how exposed a council's revenue position is to Bank Rate movements, which peers and lenders track closely.
findings.figures: £3,131k budget; £3,447k forecast outturn; £316k variance
findings.quote: Interest payable for the year is now forecast to be higher than originally budgeted.

findings.headline: Short-term debt rose £34.3 million to £88.3 million at 30 September 2026, which the paper attributes to the repayment profile of PWLB EIP loans rather than new short-term borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper says the increase is primarily from the repayment structure of Equal Interest and Principal loans, where part of the balance is reclassified as short-term each half year. It also reports long-term borrowing down £12.5 million to £245.6 million.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender reading debt maturity profiles needs to know that the short-term figure reflects reclassification of amortising loans, not a rise in refinancing need.
findings.figures: £88.3 million short-term debt; increase of £34.3 million; £245.6 million long-term debt; decrease of £12.5 million
findings.quote: The Council held £88.3 million of short-term debt at 30 September, reflecting an increase of £34.3 million from the position at the end of 2025/26.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio delivering £377k less revenue than planned, driven by vacancies and project delays
findings.detail: Economic Development commercial property revenue is forecasting £55k against a £400k proposal (£345k shortfall, rated AMBER) due to vacant units and prospective occupier engagement delays; full recovery is deferred to 2027-28. South Cambs Connect ground floor lettings are also behind plan at £18k against a £50k proposal (£32k shortfall, rated AMBER) due to ongoing work on the charging plan. Combined, the commercial property portfolio is £377k short of plan.
findings.matters: The council's commercial property portfolio is materially underperforming, affecting the reliability of commercial revenue as a funding source for its budget.
findings.figures: Economic Development: £400k proposal, £55k forecast (£345k shortfall); South Cambs Connect: £50k proposal, £18k forecast (£32k shortfall)
findings.quote: One unit remains vacant, and a further unit has recently become vacant. Work is ongoing with prospective occupiers to secure occupancy of the empty units. It is therefore anticipated that the full income will not be realised in 2026/27, with a proportion now expected to be received in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Government policy announcements (LGR and GCDC) blocking £125k of planned commercial income
findings.detail: The Local Government Reorganisation announcement has made prospective tenants unwilling to enter multi-year lease agreements, eliminating the expected £100k of rental income at South Cambs Hall (proposal to £0 forecast, rated RED). Similarly, the Greater Cambridge Development Corporation announcement has halted preparatory work for £25k of Built and Natural Environment Service additional income (proposal to £0, rated RED). Combined, these government announcements are preventing £125k of planned revenue from being realised.
findings.matters: Government policy announcements are creating material barriers to the council's revenue plans, demonstrating that external policy uncertainty directly threatens the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: South Cambs Hall: £100k proposal to £0 forecast; BNE: £25k proposal to £0 forecast
findings.quote: Due to the announcement of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), no new tenants are currently expected to occupy the vacant space, as prospective occupiers are generally unwilling to enter into lease agreements with terms of less than two years.

findings.headline: The 42% net service cost underspend is substantially explained by £1.4 million carried-forward grants and timing differences, not real budget overperformance.
findings.detail: While net service costs show £2.094m underspend (42%), the council carried £1.4m of grant income from 2025/26 into the current year. The council explicitly warns that Q1 position is not a reliable guide to final outturn, with variances largely reflecting phased service delivery and timing of income and expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender must distinguish real budget performance from timing noise; the council's transparency prevents misinterpretation of financial position.
findings.figures: £2,094,000 underspend (42% of net service costs); £1.4 million grant carry-forward from 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council has carried forward £1.4 million of grant income from 2025/26, resulting in income levels above the approved budget... The position at the end of June 202 6 is not necessarily a good guide to the final outturn and needs to be treated as such.

findings.headline: Efficiency proposals totalling £734,000 are on track with no areas of concern identified.
findings.detail: The council included £734,000 of efficiency proposals in the 2026/27 budget comprising ongoing savings and income generation. Q1 monitoring confirms no further areas of concern, indicating the planned budget reductions are being delivered.
findings.matters: A lender must verify the council's planned savings are materializing; their delivery is essential to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £734,000 efficiency proposals
findings.quote: The original budget for 202 6/27 included efficiency proposals totalling £ 734,000 comprising of ongoing savings and income generation... there are no further areas of concern at this stage.

findings.headline: General Fund investment income outperforming budget by £96k (+4% favorable variance)
findings.detail: Treasury management generated £2,313k actual investment income against £2,217k budget, a £96k outperformance in Q1. This reflects better-than-budgeted returns on cash balances, likely due to higher prevailing interest rates.
findings.matters: A lender would see better treasury returns as improving the council's cash reserves and financial resilience, though this benefit is likely temporary and dependent on interest rates remaining elevated.
findings.figures: Budgeted £2,217k; actual £2,313k; outperformance £96k

findings.headline: General Fund interest costs £165k lower than budgeted (-23% variance)
findings.detail: Interest payable came in at £556k actual against £721k budget, saving £165k in the quarter. This may reflect either lower-than-budgeted borrowing levels or interest rates lower than assumed in the budget.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know the cause: if the saving reflects lower borrowing, it may indicate constrained capital investment; if lower rates, it is a temporary benefit dependent on interest rate assumptions holding.
findings.figures: Budgeted £721k; actual £556k; saving £165k
findings.quote: Interest Payable 3,131 721 556 (165) -23%

findings.headline: HRA rent income collection £107k below budget in Q1 (1% shortfall)
findings.detail: HRA income came in at £11,697k against budget of £11,804k, a shortfall of £107k. Although small as a percentage, any adverse variance on rent collection is worth monitoring as an early signal of arrears or void problems.
findings.matters: A lender depends on rent collection trends as a leading indicator of HRA viability and debt servicing capacity. Even small collection shortfalls can compound and signal emerging problems with tenant financial resilience.
findings.figures: Budgeted income £11,804k; actual £11,697k; shortfall £107k

findings.headline: HRA full-year budget set to break even with only £11k deficit and no financial buffer
findings.detail: The HRA budgets for a £11k deficit on £46m expenditure, meaning it is set to run at break-even. This leaves the account with no margin for adverse variances. Q1 shows an £8.4m surplus, which reflects the timing of quarterly charges and rent collection against spread expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the HRA has no financial headroom. Any adverse variance on rent collection, maintenance costs, or interest rates would force the account into deficit and require reserve draw-down or emergency action mid-year.
findings.figures: Full year deficit budget £11k; Q1 surplus £8,370k
findings.quote: Deficit / (Surplus) for the Year (11) (7,447) (8,370) (923) -12%

findings.headline: HRA shared ownership home repurchase programme spent £382k more than the £150k budget (255% variance)
findings.detail: Actual spending on repurchasing HRA shared ownership homes was £532k against a budget of £150k, a £382k or 255% overspend. This discretionary capital line is running at 3.5 times budget, indicating either sharply higher takeup of the buyback scheme or higher-than-expected purchase prices.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand why a £150k budgeted programme is consuming £532k of capital. This diverts resources from planned investment and suggests either demand or price pressures the council did not anticipate.
findings.figures: Budgeted £150k; actual £532k; overspend £382k
findings.quote: Repurchase of HRA Shared Ownership Homes 150 150 532 382 255%

findings.headline: Director of Greater Cambridge Shared Planning shows £1.4m adverse variance on a £10m budget
findings.detail: The budget to date position of £760k against actual of (£645k) produced a variance of (£1,406k), recorded as -185%. This is a material swing on the joint planning service budget. If run at this rate, the full-year position could be £5-6m adverse of budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know when a major service line is running materially off forecast. Planning services generate income; a negative variance of this size signals either cost pressure or income underperformance that would constrain the council's overall position.
findings.figures: Full year budget £10,080k; Q1 variance (£1,406k) at -185%
findings.quote: Director of Greater Cambridge Shared Planning 10,080 760 (645) (1,406) -185%

findings.headline: Homelessness expenditure £40k below budget reflecting benefits of property acquisition strategy
findings.detail: Homelessness service spending is £40k under budget (-23% variance at Q1), which the council attributes to benefits from 'work undertaken in recent years to acquire single-occupancy properties for homelessness households, thereby reducing reliance on more costly bed and breakfast accommodation'. The council has flagged that it will closely monitor whether this trend continues through the financial year, suggesting awareness that this may be a timing or demand fluctuation.
findings.matters: Homelessness services are typically high-cost and volatile demand; cost control through service model change is financially positive, but the council's caveat suggests this may not be fully sustained.
findings.figures: £40k underspend, -23% variance, Q1 actual £132k versus budget £173k
findings.quote: This may reflect the benefits of work undertaken in recent years to acquire single-occupancy properties for homelessness households, thereby reducing reliance on more costly bed and breakfast accommodation. The position will continue to be closely monitored throughout the remainder of the financial year to assess whether this trend is sustained.

findings.headline: Commercial waste income £162k short of budget due to market competition and Materials Recovery Facility revenue decline
findings.detail: Greater Cambridge Shared Waste Services is £162k below profiled Q1 budget on commercial waste income (2% shortfall). The council attributes this to 'the challenging and highly competitive nature of the commercial waste market' and 'reduced income from materials sold through the councils' Materials Recovery Facility (MRF)'.
findings.matters: Market-facing waste service revenue exposes the council to commodity price and competitive pressures; actual underperformance indicates these headwinds are materializing in the current year.
findings.figures: £162k shortfall on Q1 budget, 2% variance
findings.quote: Income received at the end of Quarter 1 is below the profiled budget due to the challenging and highly competitive nature of the commercial waste market and reduced income from materials sold through the councils' Materials Recovery Facility (MRF).

findings.headline: Planning income under pressure from PPA reduction following Government Development Corporation announcement
findings.detail: Planning Performance Agreement income has fallen due to developers postponing applications following the Government's Development Corporation announcement for Greater Cambridge. The overall planning income position shows a net adverse variance of £605k (43% of Q1 budget), with the explanatory text identifying the PPA reduction as a specific factor. While Business Operations fee income exceeded budget, this did not offset the PPA weakness.
findings.matters: Planning fee income is discretionary revenue exposed to policy and economic uncertainty; a 43% variance driven by external policy change is material to budget delivery and indicates forward pressure on this revenue stream.
findings.figures: Planning income £1,414k Q1 budget, variance £605k (shown as -43%). PPA specifically identified as reduced.
findings.quote: A reduction in Planning Performance Agreement (PPA) income has been experienced due to some developers postponing application submissions following the Government's Greater Cambridge Development Corporation announcement, resulting in lower income levels than originally forecast.

findings.headline: Formal programme concluded with transition to continuous improvement model and monitoring systems for 2026/27 deliverables.
findings.detail: The formal Transformation Programme concluded in March 2026 with arrangements remaining to monitor delivery of efficiencies scheduled for implementation during 2026/27. Cabinet approved a Continuous Improvement Strategy in 2024 committing services to regularly review processes and service arrangements.
findings.matters: Ensures achieved efficiencies continue to be tracked and that the council has embedded systems for ongoing cost management.
findings.figures: Programme concluded March 2026; monitoring continues through 2026/27
findings.quote: Although the formal Transformation Programme concluded in March 2026, arrangements remain in place to monitor delivery of efficiencies scheduled for implementation during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Programme established in 2021 to address anticipated government funding reductions and ensure financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The Transformation Programme was established in 2021 in anticipation of the Government's Fair Funding Review and potential funding reductions. It was designed to generate sufficient efficiencies to cover investment costs and contribute to the Council's 5-year financial strategy.
findings.matters: Shows proactive financial planning in response to anticipated funding pressures, with a deliberate strategy to build financial resilience.
findings.figures: Established 2021; concluded March 2026; 5-year delivery period
findings.quote: The Transformation Programme was established in 2021 in anticipation of the Government's Fair Funding Review and the potential reduction in future funding available to South Cambridgeshire District Council (SCDC).

findings.headline: Waste Service delivered £1.2m efficiencies in a single year through system integration and service rationalization.
findings.detail: The Waste service review included system integration with the accountancy system and decommissioning of loss-making services (commercial skip and bin cleaning). The single service delivered £1.2m efficiencies in 25/26 through these process improvements.
findings.matters: Demonstrates accelerated delivery of major efficiencies in a single service, indicating strong programme management capability.
findings.figures: £1.2m efficiencies in 25/26
findings.quote: Overall, this service review has delivered £1.2m efficiencies in a year.

findings.headline: Commercial Waste pricing review generated £700k additional annual income through market rate analysis.
findings.detail: The Waste Service review found commercial waste pricing had fallen behind market levels. A comprehensive market rate analysis and multi-year pricing revision were implemented while system integration generated £392,000 one-off income in 25/26 and ongoing increases of £232,000 annually.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council's ability to identify and capture additional sustainable revenue streams, strengthening financial resilience.
findings.figures: £700,000 annual income increase; £392,000 one-off; £232,000 ongoing annual increase
findings.quote: A multi-year pricing revision was therefore implemented which enabled the service to bring prices more in line with current market levels whilst minimising the impact on existing customers. This has delivered an annual increase in income of around £700,000.

findings.headline: Transformation programme delivered £11.9m efficiencies over five years against £4.3m investment costs.
findings.detail: The Council-wide Transformation Programme concluded its formal service review phase in March 2026 after delivering £11.9m in efficiencies over five years, with £8.6m directly benefiting SCDC. The programme cost £4.3m funded through the Transformation Reserve.
findings.matters: Shows the council has successfully implemented a strategic investment that more than paid for itself, supporting medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £11.924m total 5-year efficiencies; £8.652m SCDC-specific; £4.296m 5-year costs
findings.quote: Over the five-year period, the programme has helped deliver efficiencies of approximately £11.9 million, of which more than £8.6 million directly benefits SCDC.

findings.headline: Planning payment processing reduced contact centre demand by 87%
findings.detail: Payment-related contact centre calls have fallen by 87% through automated payment visibility and processing. A Power BI dashboard now automatically reconciles 85% of planning payments instantly, replacing manual reconciliation workflows.
findings.matters: Automation of high-volume transactional processes reduces back-office costs and staffing pressure, signalling effective financial management.
findings.figures: 87% reduction in payment calls; 85% of payments automatically reconciled
findings.quote: Payment calls to the contact centre have reduced by over 87%

findings.headline: Pre-Application Service achieves cost-recovery by doubling income
findings.detail: The Pre-Application Service has moved from a subsidized service to full cost-recovery by doubling its income. Validation time has been halved through automation and improved processes. This transition frees council resources previously allocated to funding the service shortfall.
findings.matters: A service moving from subsidy-dependent to self-funding status improves the council's financial sustainability and reduces resource drain.
findings.figures: Income doubled; validation time reduced by half
findings.quote: Doubled the income to make the service cost recoverable

findings.headline: Waste service food waste rollout costs 6% more than forecast during programme implementation
findings.detail: Greater Cambridge Shared Waste Service spent £2,091k against Q1 budget of £1,965k (£126k or 6% overspend) on increased food waste collection expenditure during rollout. The council states the full cost is covered by grant funding.
findings.matters: Grant-funded overspend mitigates immediate risk, but rising rollout costs signal forecasting gaps; if future phases require council funding, the cost escalation pattern becomes material to affordability planning.
findings.figures: Budget £1,965k, Actual £2,091k, variance £126k (6%)
findings.quote: There has been increased expenditure on the provision of food waste collection service during the programme rollout compared with the budgeted forecast. The full cost is funded by grant monies.

findings.headline: Unplanned fire damage at council housing property drives £122k maintenance cost overspend
findings.detail: Housing stock improvement budget overran by 8% in Q1 (£122k overspend) entirely due to emergency works following fire damage at one property. This unplanned emergency maintenance consumed 8% of the quarterly maintenance allocation.
findings.matters: Emergency maintenance costs are a credit indicator; they disrupt planned spending, may signal building condition risks requiring ongoing additional investment, and reduce the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Quarterly budget £1,490k, Actual £1,612k, variance £122k (8%)
findings.quote: The Quarter 1 variance is attributable to unplanned works required at one of the Council's properties following fire damage, resulting in expenditure above the budget profile.

findings.headline: Shared Ownership repurchase programme massively overruns Q1 budget as demand exceeds forecast
findings.detail: The council budgeted £150k for Q1 Shared Ownership repurchases but spent £532k, a 255% overspend. Three properties were acquired during the quarter. The budget is explicitly demand-led, indicating the council's forecasts for this line significantly underestimated acquisition demand.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs forecasting accuracy; a demand-led capital programme overrunning 255% in one quarter suggests budget assumptions are unreliable and exposes cash flow risks.
findings.figures: Budget £150k, Actual £532k, variance £382k (255%)
findings.quote: The budget is demand-led, with expenditure dependent on both the number of homes re-presented to the Council and the acquisition values. During Quarter 1, three Shared Ownership properties were acquired and will be marketed for sale, contributing to the variance against the budget profile.

findings.headline: Local government reorganization will create organizational uncertainty with potential strain on audit oversight capacity
findings.detail: The council's internal audit function warns that planned local government reorganization will create a period of heightened uncertainty and significant system transition. The audit team explicitly flags that demand for advisory work may exceed their currently planned resources during this transition, requiring difficult prioritization of what auditing work can be completed.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence that governance and controls remain effective during major organizational disruption; under-resourced audit oversight during significant change is a risk factor.
findings.figures: Audit team: four qualified auditors and one audit assistant. Current resources sufficient for 'typical risk-based plan' but must be reviewed given LGR demands.
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) will impact the Council's governance, risk, and control environment. It introduces a period of heightened uncertainty, organisational change, and significant system transition.

findings.headline: A Local Government Reorganisation is pending and will require governance arrangements to be reconsidered
findings.detail: The council notes that the 2025/2026 AGS will need to reflect the outcome of a Local Government Reorganisation once known. In preparation, the council is undertaking a deeper periodic review of its governance code and arrangements. The paper does not specify the nature, timing, or scope of this reorganisation.
findings.matters: Local Government Reorganisations can materially affect council structure, financial arrangements, and service delivery capacity, all relevant to credit assessment.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The 2025/2026 AGS will need to reflect the outcome of the Local Government Reorganisation once this is known. In addition to our regular planned cyclical review of the Code, we are undertaking a periodic deeper review of the contents. This will help provide assurance as part of the preparation for Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: £61.815m increase in property, plant and equipment, primarily house building and Northstowe construction
findings.detail: Capital expenditure drove a large increase in fixed assets, concentrated on council dwellings and assets under construction as part of the house building programme and Northstowe community facilities.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments to housing development carry delivery and operational risk; lenders track the scale and progress of such schemes.
findings.figures: £61.815m increase in PP&E
findings.quote: The largest figure, unsurprisingly, relates to Property Plant and Equipment which has increased by £ 61.815m on the prior year. This was caused by significantly more capital expenditure in 2025/26 relating to Council dwellings and assets under construction. This primarily relates to the house building programme and community facilities at Nortstowe

findings.headline: Investment property valuations rose less than prior year, coinciding with overall surplus decline
findings.detail: The council reports investment property values increased less in 2025-26 than 2024-25, and the overall CIES surplus fell from £28.941m to £21.828m. This suggests property market conditions may be softening.
findings.matters: Weakening property valuations affect the council's investment income and balance sheet strength, which lenders monitor.
findings.figures: CIES surplus down £7.1m to £21.828m; investment property revaluation described as 'less marked'
findings.quote: The increase in the value of the Council's investment property in 2025/26 was less marked than in the prior year

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account surplus fell from £7.845m to £0.567m in 2025-26
findings.detail: The HRA surplus fell from £7.845m to £0.567m. The paper presents this as fact but offers no explanation for the collapse. This could indicate rising repair costs, rent arrears, void properties, or asset write-downs in the housing business.
findings.matters: A sudden 93% drop in HRA surplus signals operational problems in the council's rental housing that could strain overall finances and would interest lenders assessing housing asset performance.
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account saw a surplus of £0.567m for the year compared to a surplus of 7.845m in the prior year.

findings.headline: Bank of England signalled potential rate increases ahead if inflation persists, creating downside risk to council's financial forecasts.
findings.detail: Base rate was held at 3.75% contrary to budget expectations of further cuts. Bank of England cited persistent inflation above 2% target and signalled possibility of future increases, contradicting assumptions in medium-term financial planning.
findings.matters: Inability to forecast interest rate direction undermines medium-term budget certainty; rate increases would directly amplify debt servicing costs on £312m debt portfolio at currently uncertain rates.
findings.figures: Base rate held at 3.75% after 3 cuts early in year; £312.123m total external debt exposed to future rate movements
findings.quote: The increased uncertainty and inflation remaining above the 2% target have led to the Bank of England leaving rates unchanged with the possibility that rates may need to increase if inflationary pressures persist.

findings.headline: Interest costs rose unexpectedly in Q4 due to geopolitical volatility, contradicting budget forecasts of further rate cuts.
findings.detail: Interest payments exceeded budget by £50k (£2.846m actual vs £2.796m budgeted) due to Q4 cost increases. Original 2025/26 budget had assumed further Bank of England rate cuts that did not materialise.
findings.matters: Unexpected cost increases demonstrate vulnerability to external shocks and indicate budget forecasting risk; geopolitical events outside council control directly increase debt servicing costs.
findings.figures: Interest variance: £50k overspend (£2.846m actual vs £2.796m budgeted)
findings.quote: Borrowing costs rose in Q4, largely driven by market volatility following the escalation of tensions in the Middle East involving the USA and Iran.

findings.headline: Property development loan of £15.774m has principal and interest repayment deferred until property occupation occurs.
findings.detail: South Cambridgeshire Investment Partnership (SCIP) loan has no repayment schedule for principal or interest until properties are occupied. This represents capital locked up in development with timing risk.
findings.matters: Capital committed to property development creates illiquidity; delays in property occupation directly reduce cash available for reserves and create timing mismatch with debt obligations.
findings.figures: SCIP: £15.774m at 1.50% interest; represents 11% of long-term portfolio
findings.quote: Repayment (Principal and Interest) will not begin until the properties are occupied

findings.headline: Largest single investment (£119m to own company) has repayment terms still "To be agreed" with no maturity date set.
findings.detail: Ermine Street Housing loan represents 80% of the council's long-term investment portfolio, held on interest-only basis at 4.08%. The final repayment date remains undefined despite being the council's largest asset commitment, creating cash flow uncertainty.
findings.matters: Undefined repayment of the council's largest investment suggests either the company cannot afford repayment or governance weakness in not settling terms; materially affects balance sheet clarity and liquidity planning.
findings.figures: Ermine Street Housing: £119.028m at 4.08% interest only; represents 80% of £136.869m long-term portfolio
findings.quote: Ermine Street Housing  119,028 Interest only payable quarterly On schedule To be agreed 4.08

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased by £44.858m (11%) in a single year, signalling substantial capital programmes requiring future borrowing.
findings.detail: The CFR grew from £409.181m to £454.039m, a 10.9% increase. Total external debt rose to £312.123m, up £34m. The council is funding this through a combination of external borrowing and internal resources, with £10m PWLB debt repaid but offset by larger increases.
findings.matters: An 11% annual increase in capital financing requirement directly drives future borrowing needs and debt servicing costs, constraining affordability; this trajectory matters for debt sustainability.
findings.figures: CFR: £409.181m → £454.039m (£44.858m increase); total external debt: £312.123m (up from £278.123m)
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) has increased in the period to 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Business rates levy forecasting error of £1.13m despite revised budget indicates income volatility
findings.detail: The Business Rates levy payable to the pool was £1.13m higher than the revised budget, despite being prepared partway through the year with more current information. The paper explicitly notes business rates 'remains inherently difficult to forecast with precision,' highlighting ongoing forecast challenges on this material income source.
findings.matters: Business rates are a major local government income source; material forecast errors of this magnitude on a revised budget indicate the council cannot reliably predict this income component, affecting financial planning stability
findings.figures: Business Rates levy overspend: £1.13m higher than revised budget
findings.quote: Business rates income remains inherently difficult to forecast with precision and is therefore estimated at the beginning of the year for the General Fund. For 2025/26, the Business Rates levy payable to the Pool Account was £ 1.13 million higher than anticipated in the revised budget.

findings.headline: Business rates pool gains of £2.038m will cease from 2026-27 onwards due to BRRS reset
findings.detail: The council received £2.038m from the Cambridgeshire & Peterborough business rates pool in 2025-26, exceeding budget by £19k. The paper explicitly states these gains will terminate when the Business Rates Retention Scheme resets. This represents the loss of approximately £2m annual income that must be absorbed in future financial planning.
findings.matters: Business rates pooling has provided material annual funding; loss of this income stream from 2026-27 onwards represents a significant future funding pressure requiring careful medium-term financial planning
findings.figures: Business rates pool gain 2025-26: £2.038m (budgeted £2.019m); income ceases from 2026-27
findings.quote: However, this will not continue beyond 2025/26, as the BRRS reset removes the financial benefits of current pooling arrangements.

findings.headline: Multiple capital projects delayed with £1.031m total underspend carried forward into future years
findings.detail: Food waste collection service running £542k behind schedule, continuing across three phases into 2026-27. Cambridge Science Park roof replacement delayed by overhead power line constraints (£117k underspend). South Cambridgeshire Hall construction rephased following updated condition survey (£225k underspend). Pattern indicates delivery challenges extending project completion timescales.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays indicate execution risk and affect the council's ability to deliver planned infrastructure and service improvements on committed schedules
findings.figures: Total capital underspend: £1.031m; Food waste: £542k; Cambridge Science Park: £117k; South Cambridgeshire Hall: £225k
findings.quote: Expenditure on the food waste collection service was £542,000 below budget. Implementation is ongoing and will continue across three further phases during 2026/27 to achieve full district-wide coverage.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs increased by £357k in Q4 due to elevated interest rates
findings.detail: Interest payable exceeded revised budget by £357k (10.86% variance). The paper attributes this specifically to elevated interest rates in the final quarter of 2025/26, combined with increased Minimum Revenue Provision charges. This represents a material increase in debt servicing costs driven by external market conditions and signals ongoing exposure to rate-driven cost pressures.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand how rising interest rates affect the council's debt servicing trajectory and future borrowing capacity
findings.figures: Interest Payable: revised budget £3,288k, outturn £3,645k = £357k overspend (10.86%)
findings.quote: higher-than-anticipated borrowing costs and increased Accounting Reversals / Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charges, driven by the elevated interest rate environment in the final quarter of 2025/26

findings.headline: £40m PWLB borrowing at unusually short 2-3 year terms for long-term housing assets
findings.detail: The council borrowed £40m via PWLB with repayment terms of only 2-3 years made half-yearly. This creates significant refinancing risk and near-term cash flow pressure, as housing assets typically require much longer-term financing (15-30 years).
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing for long-term assets creates refinancing risk if rates rise, puts large repayment obligations on the already thin reserves, and suggests constrained access to conventional longer-term financing.
findings.figures: PWLB borrowing: £40m; terms: 2-3 years; repayment: half-yearly
findings.quote: There was additional borrowing of £40 million in 2025/26 through Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) loans to support the New Build Programme. These loans have terms of two to three years, with repayments made on a half -yearly basis over their duration.

findings.headline: £11.3m of new build housing spending slipped to 2026-27 due to unfinalised developer contracts
findings.detail: The New Build Programme experienced £11.305m of underspend (18% of the £62.5m budget). Two major schemes—Northstowe Station Road and Southern Gardens Waterbeach—suffered delays because developer contracts had not been finalised by year-end, with six other schemes also experiencing programme slippage.
findings.matters: Significant delivery delays raise questions about project management and developer partnership. The council has borrowed £40m for this programme but spent substantially less, tying up cash while carrying forward repayment obligations.
findings.figures: New Build underspend: £11.305m; Northstowe Station Road: £2.990m; Southern Gardens Waterbeach: £0.988m; Sawston Tudor Meadow: £1.821m; Barrington Phase 3: £2.091m; Cambourne SCIP: £2.433m; Marleigh Fen Ditton: £1.191m
findings.quote: Two developments experienced delays as contracts had not been finalised with developers by 31 March 2026: Northstowe, Station Road £2.990 million, Southern Gardens, Waterbeach £0.988 million

findings.headline: General HRA reserve has fallen to minimum level with required further drawdowns in 2026-27
findings.detail: The General HRA reserve decreased to £3.503m, which the council explicitly states is just above its minimum level of £3.5m, leaving almost no buffer. The council withdrew £2.0m from its Self-Financing earmarked reserve in 2025-26 to maintain this minimum, and the report indicates further drawdowns will be required in 2026-27 to support the capital programme.
findings.matters: Thin reserves with structural reliance on drawdowns indicate limited shock absorption capacity for unexpected costs (repairs, arrears, void properties) and suggest the HRA cannot sustain itself on revenue income alone.
findings.figures: General HRA reserve: £3.503m (minimum: £3.5m); Self-Financing reserve withdrawal: £2.0m
findings.quote: During 2025/26, there was no usage or addition to the insurance reserve but £2.0 million was withdrawn from the Self-Financing reserve to maintain the General HRA reserve balance above the minimum level of £3.5 million

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report - Quarter end 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Interest rate markets have shifted from expecting falls to pricing in potential rises
findings.detail: Base rate fell from 4.50% to 3.75% in the first three quarters of 2025/26, but the Council reports market reversal: 'the current conflict in the Middle East has seen Markets reverse sentiment and are now pricing in the possibility of base rate increases should hostilities continue and inflation pressures rise.' This threatens to erode investment returns and increase future borrowing costs.
findings.matters: The Council's investment income forecast of £6.8m depends on rates staying higher than the budget assumption. Interest rate rises would reduce returns; falls would increase borrowing costs on refinance.
findings.figures: Base rate fell from 4.50% to 3.75%; Council achieved 4.12% blended return Q3; budgeted investment income £6.8m
findings.quote: the current conflict in the Middle East has seen Markets reverse sentiment and are now pricing in the possibility of base rate increases should hostilities continue and inflation pressures rise

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report - Quarter end 31 December 2025
findings.headline: 69% of long-term investment portfolio is concentrated in single housing association
findings.detail: Ermine Street Housing holds £119.2m of £136m in long-term investments. The loan is performing (on schedule, yielding 4.09%) but concentration in a single counterparty means financial stress at Ermine Street Housing would immediately impact the Council's liquidity.
findings.matters: Concentration risk means the Council's investment position is vulnerable to a single counterparty failure; lenders monitor this as a potential drain on available reserves.
findings.figures: Ermine Street Housing: £119.2m of £136.2m long-term investments (69%)
findings.quote: Ermine St Housing  119,213 69%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report - Quarter end 31 December 2025
findings.headline: £14.7m loan to SCIP has repayment deferred until properties are occupied
findings.detail: The South Cambridgeshire Investment Partnership holds a £14.7m loan with no repayment of principal or interest until properties it is funding are occupied. This creates timing uncertainty: if occupation is delayed, the Council's cash recovery is delayed and refinancing risk emerges.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand when cash will be recovered from major investments. Deferred recovery based on occupancy dates introduces refinancing risk if timelines slip.
findings.figures: £14.7m outstanding; 9% of investment portfolio; 1.50% interest rate; repayment status: N/A
findings.quote: Repayment (Principal and Interest) will not begin until the properties are occupied

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report - Quarter end 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Significant borrowing increase to fund New Build Housing Programme
findings.detail: Council increased total borrowing from £278.1m (31 March 2025) to £317.1m (31 December 2025)—an increase of £39m in nine months. Of this, short-term borrowing increased £22m and long-term borrowing £17m. The increase funds the housing programme and includes short-term borrowing taken in December for refinancing.
findings.matters: A material increase in leverage in nine months is significant to lenders assessing the Council's debt trajectory and its ability to service housing programme borrowing from scheme returns.
findings.figures: Total borrowing increased from £278.1m to £317.1m; short-term borrowing up £22m to £68m; long-term borrowing up £17m to £249.1m
findings.quote: This increase in borrowing is to fund the New Build Housing Programme and short term debt was obtained in December before refinancing with long-term debt from PWLB in Quarter 4.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is compressing transformation timescales and increasing delivery risk
findings.detail: Local Government Reorganisation discussions are ongoing (Cambridgeshire & Peterborough unitary proposal). The compressed timeline is forcing the council to accelerate its organisational review and transformation programme. The residual likelihood score on operational delivery increased from 2 to 3 in Sept 2025 specifically because of this timescale pressure.
findings.matters: Organisational disruption during a compressed transformation can delay service improvements, delay realisation of efficiency savings, create staff uncertainty, and reduce service quality during transition.
findings.figures: Organisational review: residual likelihood increased from 2 to 3; residual risk now 9; LGR risk residual score 9 (inherent 16)
findings.quote: Residual Likelihood has increased from a 2 to a 3 due to the reduction in timescale as a result of Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Housing land supply has fallen to 4.6 years, below the statutory 5-year requirement
findings.detail: South Cambridgeshire can now only demonstrate 4.6 years of available housing land for delivery, down from 6.5 years. This triggers the NPPF 'tilted balance', which favors development applications and reduces the council's planning control over development types and sequencing. The council is working to increase delivery through planning permissions and working with house builders.
findings.matters: A falling land supply reduces the council's control over the type and location of development, and can result in unplanned sprawl or infrastructure strain.
findings.figures: Land supply: 4.6 years vs 5-year requirement; residual risk 12 (amber); likelihood improved from 4 to 3 in Sept 2025 based on current 5-year land supply position
findings.quote: The NPPF provides a tilted balance in favour of development applications, leading to a potential reduction in control in relation to the type of development taking place in the district.

findings.headline: New social housing regulations are forcing spending choices between stock maintenance and new builds
findings.detail: Social housing regulation changes require higher spending on repairs, safety compliance, and tenant satisfaction measures on existing council stock. This creates pressure to reduce new build delivery to stay within capital budgets. A mock inspection in Sept/Oct 2025 identified compliance gaps requiring remedial spending.
findings.matters: Regulatory spending demands on existing assets leave less capacity for income-generating new builds or economic growth projects. This constrains revenue growth.
findings.figures: Risk residual score 8 (improved from inherent 16); council secured £8.2m SHDF funding for decarbonisation; 10-year rent settlement at CPI+1% agreed with government
findings.quote: Potential trade-offs in priorities, such as reduction in the number of new council rented homes and shared ownership homes being delivered to offset spend on maintaining existing homes to meet new regulative requirements

findings.headline: Government withdrew funding for wastewater treatment plant relocation, directly constraining growth infrastructure
findings.detail: The council had planned to rely on government funding for wastewater treatment relocation to enable housing growth in the Cambridge area. Government withdrew this funding in late 2025. The council is now seeking solutions through DEFRA, MHCLG, and water companies, but the constraint remains unresolved and blocks planned infrastructure.
findings.matters: Infrastructure constraints directly limit housing delivery, which limits growth in the local tax base and development-related income the council can generate.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 4, inherent 16; government funding withdrawal noted in Feb 2026 update; Water Resources Management Plan submitted to DEFRA but capacity still uncertain
findings.quote: An update was provided to Members on the impacts of the recent decision from government to withdraw funding for the relocation of the Waste Water Treatment Plant (late 2025).

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs remain a significant, sustained overspend on statutory obligations
findings.detail: The council has a statutory duty to house homeless people, and demand is rising due to cost of living pressures, refugee support, and housing affordability. The council budgets for significant overspend here. Despite controls including properties purchased through LAFH funding and partnerships with housing providers, this risk is held at amber level, meaning material ongoing costs are expected.
findings.matters: Statutory spending that exceeds budget must be funded from reserves or diverted from other priorities, reducing financial flexibility and eroding available reserves.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 12 (amber, same as last review in Dec 2025); inherent risk 20; controls include £8.2m SHDF funding and government grants
findings.quote: Significant overspend on temporary accommodation budget due to statutory obligations.

findings.headline: Expenditure accrual control weakness: at least one 2024-25 invoice received in 2025-26 was not accrued in correct period
findings.detail: During testing of year-end accruals, the auditor identified at least one transaction where an expenditure invoice for 2024-25 was received in 2025-26 with no accrual posted in the relevant financial period. This was subsequently corrected by management, but indicates the accrual process may not be capturing all amounts that should be accrued.
findings.matters: Incomplete accrual recording understates year-end liabilities, overstates reserves, and misrepresents the council's true financial position to lenders and stakeholders.
findings.figures: At least one material accrual omission identified and corrected
findings.quote: One transaction was identified where an expenditure invoice relating to 2024/25 was received in 2025/26, however no accrual was posted in the relevant financial period. This was corrected by management

findings.headline: Staff unavailability prevented completion of property asset audit procedures due to backstop deadline
findings.detail: Significant delays in completing audit work on property, plant and equipment resulted from unavailability of entity staff. This prevented the auditor from verifying the accuracy of data provided to valuers, which cascaded into inability to complete the reserves audit work ahead of the backstop date.
findings.matters: Property typically comprises the largest portion of a council's asset base. Unverified property valuations undermine balance sheet reliability and reserve calculations.
findings.figures: Property, plant and equipment audit procedures incomplete
findings.quote: Significant delays due to unavailability of entity staff in relation to property, plant and equipment

findings.headline: No key controls in place around pension liability assumptions; £0.7m difference between assumed and actual returns identified
findings.detail: The audit found no key controls around the assumptions underpinning the council's pension liability valuation. Although management reviews assumptions, they do not actively challenge them or assess the reasonableness of calculations. The auditor identified that the actuaries used an estimated rate of return on pension assets that differed from actual returns by £0.7m, which management has corrected.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are typically a council's largest liability. Weak controls allow assumptions to drift from reality; the £0.7m variance demonstrates the materiality of estimation errors.
findings.figures: £0.7m difference between estimated and actual return on pension assets (corrected)
